props.title: Jumping the Broom
props.initialSlug: Two families clash at a Martha's Vineyard wedding

sections.content: **Jumping the Broom (2011)** (2011) exemplifies the evolution of African-American wedding films, blending cultural traditions with class conflict. Like **The Best Man** (1999) and **Soul Food** (1997), it explores family dynamics within the Black upper middle class, but adds the specific tension between old customs and new money. Director Salim Akil tackles the clash between Martha's Vineyard affluence and working-class Brooklyn values, using the traditional jumping the broom ceremony as both a literal plot point and metaphor for bridging divides.

movies.title: Why Did I Get Married?
movies.slug: Tyler Perry's exploration of four couples confronting relationship challenges during an annual retreat

sections.content: The film follows a pattern established by earlier Black romantic ensemble pieces like **Love Jones** (1997) and **Brown Sugar** (2002), where relationship drama serves as a lens to examine broader social issues. But **Jumping the Broom** distinguishes itself by directly addressing class tensions within the African-American community, something rarely tackled so explicitly in mainstream romantic comedies. The performances of Angela Bassett and Loretta Devine as clashing mothers-in-law elevate what could have been standard wedding movie tropes into a nuanced examination of generational and social divides.

Wedding films centered on Black families gained significant momentum in the 2010s, with **Think Like a Man** (2012) and **The Best Man Holiday** (2013) following similar themes of love across class lines. **Jumping the Broom** stands out for its specific focus on African-American traditions and their modern interpretations, while maintaining the glossy production values and ensemble cast dynamics that made films like **Father of the Bride** (1991) successful. sections.content: The film's treatment of the jumping the broom tradition connects to a larger cinematic conversation about preserving cultural practices in contemporary settings. Like **Coming to America** (1988) and more recently **Crazy Rich Asians** (2018), the movie uses wedding customs as a way to explore cultural identity. The Martha's Vineyard setting deliberately places Black wealth and tradition in a space historically associated with white affluence, similar to how **The Best Man** (1999) positioned its characters in upscale New York professional circles.
